All three answered from the source (the `.claude/knowledge/` KB confirms each).

## 1. Does `deleteComment` verify who wrote the comment?

**No — and it structurally can't.**

`ArticleService.deleteComment(slug, id)` (`src/article/article.service.ts:114`) takes only a slug and a comment id. It loads the article, finds the comment by id in `article.comments`, splices it out, and deletes it. No caller identity is involved at any point.

The controller confirms it (`src/article/article.controller.ts:85`):
```ts
@Delete(':slug/comments/:id')
async deleteComment(@Param() params) {
  const {slug, id} = params;
  return await this.articleService.deleteComment(slug, id);
}
```
There is no `@User('id')` param — the handler never even learns who is calling.

The root cause is the schema: `Comment` (`src/article/comment.entity.ts`) has only `id`, `body`, and a `@ManyToOne` back to `ArticleEntity`. **There is no author column**, so there is nothing to compare a caller against even if you wanted to.

What *is* enforced: `ArticleModule` puts `AuthMiddleware` on `DELETE /articles/:slug/comments/:id`, so you need a valid token. Any authenticated user can delete any comment on any article. The `@ApiResponse({ status: 403 })` decorator on line 83 describes intent, not behavior — nothing in the path returns 403. (The KB flags this as part of a broader pattern: ownership is enforced *nowhere* in this codebase.)

## 2. Profile routes with `AuthMiddleware`

From `src/profile/profile.module.ts:19-23` — one rule, covering all methods:

```ts
consumer
  .apply(AuthMiddleware)
  .forRoutes({path: 'profiles/:username/follow', method: RequestMethod.ALL});
```

| Route | Handler | Guarded |
|---|---|---|
| `POST /profiles/:username/follow` | `follow()` | ✅ yes |
| `DELETE /profiles/:username/follow` | `unFollow()` | ✅ yes |
| `GET /profiles/:username` | `getProfile()` | ❌ **public** |

Note the asymmetry on the public one: `getProfile` takes `@User('id') userId`, but with no middleware that value comes from the `@User()` decorator decoding the token itself — so it's `undefined` when no token is sent. The route works anonymously but `following` won't be computed for a real viewer.

(Routes are all under the `api` global prefix from `src/main.ts`, so really `/api/profiles/...`.)

## 3. What `RO` means

**Response Object.** It marks the RealWorld API envelope type — the wrapper shape a controller returns, as opposed to the inner data interface.

The pattern is consistent across modules: an inner `*Data` interface (or a raw entity) plus an `*RO` wrapper keyed by the resource name.

| Type | Shape | File |
|---|---|---|
| `ArticleRO` | `{ article: ArticleEntity }` | `src/article/article.interface.ts:24` |
| `ArticlesRO` | `{ articles: [...], articlesCount: n }` | `article.interface.ts:28` |
| `CommentsRO` | `{ comments: Comment[] }` | `article.interface.ts:20` |
| `UserRO` | `{ user: UserData }` (includes `token`) | `src/user/user.interface.ts:9` |
| `ProfileRO` | `{ profile: ProfileData }` | `src/profile/profile.interface.ts:8` |

This isn't cosmetic — it's the client contract. RealWorld frontends read `response.article.slug`, `response.user.token`, etc., so a handler that returns a bare entity instead of the envelope breaks every RealWorld client. The mirror-image convention applies to requests: handlers read `@Body('article')` / `@Body('user')` / `@Body('comment')`, so bodies are nested the same way.

One inconsistency worth knowing: `ArticleRO` wraps the raw `ArticleEntity`, not the `ArticleData` interface declared just above it in the same file — `ArticleData` and the local `Comment` interface are declared but unused by the exported ROs.
